title: Peppa Pig owners win copyright battle against YouTube animation Wolfoo
description: In a ruling this week, the judge said "all videos featuring Wolfoo" must be taken down before 16:00 BST on Monday.Hasbro and Peppa Pig's creators Astl
body: In a ruling this week, the judge said "all videos featuring Wolfoo" must be taken down before 16:00 BST on Monday.Hasbro and Peppa Pig's creators Astley Baker Davies Ltd originally took court action in London in 2022.They claimed SConnect had attempted "to deceive the young Wolfoo viewership, most aged between two and five, into believing that Wolfoo is the same character as Peppa Pig" or connected to Peppa, the judge wrote.The companies initially complained about Wolfoo's appearance and artwork, but focused their legal case on the audio because they believed it would be easier to prove that sound clips were directly copied.The evidence of "copying of the audio clips is compelling", the judge decided."That copying was extensive, seemingly endemic at least so far as the English language Wolfoo videos are concerned."SConnect denied the copyright infringement claim but accepted that some Wolfoo videos made before mid-2020 included audio from Peppa Pig because an independent third-party contractor had used the clips without the company's knowledge.SConnect said all infringing videos were removed, and that Wolfoo animations made after mid-2020 used only voices and sounds that were created in-house.However, the judge said the fact the sounds were supplied by a third party was "irrelevant"; that while many infringing videos were removed, some were simply moved to other channels; and that the claim that all new sounds were recorded in-house "can be disproved".BBC News has asked SConnect for comment.The judge said clips from Peppa Pig were found in all 92 English-language Wolfoo videos that were examined, and about 75% of the foreign-language videos.SConnect said the ruling should only apply to the videos examined in the sample, but the judge declared that all Wolfoo videos should now be removed.SConnect also argued that the area covered by the ruling would be "too broad", but the judge said it would apply in the UK, European Union and all 166 World Trade Organisation member states, which also include the USA and Vietnam.Andrew Lee, partner and head of intellectual property at law firm Brandsmiths, which represented Hasbro, told BBC News it was a "significant judgment".Peppa Pig is available "in hundreds of countries around the world, and this was obviously a major problem for the brand because of the scale of Wolfoo", he said."By bringing the claim in the UK courts, which was our home territory, and because the defendants had activity in the United Kingdom even though they were based in Vietnam, we were able to persuade the court to hear the case on a wider scale."So it was about trying to protect the Peppa Pig brand in one forum, rather than having to bring actions in every single country."

schema.headline: Peppa Pig owners win copyright battle against YouTube animation Wolfoo

title: Andy Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care
description: In an emotional speech he praised those caring for his father, who has Alzheimer's, and said he wanted to deliver changes to help "my dad and the mill
body: In an emotional speech he praised those caring for his father, who has Alzheimer's, and said he wanted to deliver changes to help "my dad and the millions like him".Speaking to reporters afterwards, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets to fund the reforms."I think we owe it to the public before we talk about tax rises.. you first have to look the public in the eye and say 'Are we doing everything we can do from within what we've got?'"For example, he said his announcements on improving pay and training for the social care workforce "will be fully funded".But he added that fuller reforms "will require difficult decisions" and these "would be put before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people's consent".Burnham said in "an ideal world" he would not want anyone to have to sell their home to pay for care, describing it as a "really awful process".He added proposals he previously put forward, when he was health secretary in 2009, were intended to stop that, saying: "If everybody on the NHS principle contributed a little, it would mean everybody could protect the majority of what they'd worked for."He later held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and Conservative shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to get cross-party backing for any changes. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch was unavailable.The Conservatives have previously urged the prime minister to rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to pay for social care changes.Speaking to the BBC's Radio 4 PM, Andrew said it had been important to set "red lines" around funding.He acknowledged finding funding would be a "challenge" but added that there was "a significant amount of money in the system - it's just sometime it is not in the right place".Burnham did not invite the leaders of Reform UK or the Green Party of England and Wales to the talks. Both parties have expressed disappointment at this.The PM said there was a feeling at Westminster that social care was "too big a political risk" to deal with, adding he wants to take on the challenge as the "risks of failing to act are too great".Burnham highlighted the financial impact of care costs on people and spoke of how fixing issues in social care could ease the pressure on the NHS and make savings.The PM said Baroness Casey's review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding there needs to a system that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.Burnham said he wants to "immediately" focus on the social care workforce, noting a fair pay agreement is due to come into force from 2028/29 and described it as a "massive building block of a national care service".On the cross-party talks, Burnham said there has been 22 failed attempts to make progress in almost 30 years.The PM said: "We're going to have to find common ground here if this is to be a lasting solution."Lib Dem leader Sir Ed said the first "constructive" discussion had left him feeling "hopeful" and more meetings will be required to find consensus.He said: "Everyone will have to accept things we might not like in order to work together - but I think that's what the public want and expect us to do."Sir Ed, who has a disabled son who needs round-the-clock care, said the system "just isn't working" and any solution must have family carers "at its heart".Reform UK leader -and the party's health spokesman - Nigel Farage said Reform had not been invited to the talks because the government "don't want to hear a fresh, reforming voice".Asked how a new plan should be funded, Farage said his party would oppose a "death tax" and argued that "efficiencies" could be found that would make social care cheaper.He also argued that adult social care should be delivered by local councils not "centralised in Whitehall".Green Party social care spokesperson Ellie Chowns said: "If Andy Burnham is serious about doing things differently and tackling the crisis in care, he must work collaboratively with the Greens and other parties to do so."

schema.headline: Andy Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care

title: Chicken Shop Date's Amelia Dimoldenberg: I wouldn't invite Andy Burnham on my show - but I'd love a chat
description: Amelia Dimoldenberg is the queen of the deadpan silence.But when I ask her if she would ever invite the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, on to her wi
body: Amelia Dimoldenberg is the queen of the deadpan silence.But when I ask her if she would ever invite the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, on to her wildly popular YouTube series, she doesn't skip a beat."I don't think that maybe he's my type for Chicken Shop Date," she declares.That might disappoint "social first" Burnham, who's made it clear he plans to court content creators to help get his message out.Still, Dimoldenberg - who has become one of the UK's best-known content creators with millions of followers - says she's not against the idea of the prime minister collaborating with people like her, and in fact would "love" a chat with him.While some warn it's a way of dodging serious scrutiny of policies, she views it as "a positive thing" to be working with social media influencers, "because that is now where so many people get their news"."I don't think it means he's only going to be speaking to vloggers forever, really," she adds.I meet Dimoldenberg not in a chicken shop, but in a studio in BBC Broadcasting House in central London. She's OK with that though ("I love the pot plants," she says. "It's fantastic. I'm very happy to be here.")It's been more than a decade since she set up Chicken Shop Date. Since then, she's interviewed everyone from Cher to Ed Sheeran, and has become a celebrity in her own right.The show is based around her trademark dry, awkward flirting style. In person, I find her inscrutable. You get the sense she's judging your questions (I was secretly relieved when she told me later they were great).But she visibly lights up when talking about her free summer course, the Dimz Inc. Academy, which she launched to train up people aged 18-24 and help them get into the creative industries.The course offers guaranteed paid work placements, mentoring and an opportunity to gain experience across digital media. She is now bringing it back for a second year, and has extended it from one week to four."I started Chicken Shop Date as part of a youth club, and we made a magazine, and everything I learned there, the connections I made, the mentoring I got, set me up for the career that I have today," she explains."So it was always such a big ambition of mine to be able to give that back to young people when I was able to."Behind it is a serious issue. Dimoldenberg points to the high number of young people not in employment, education or training - a group known as Neets. "That's really a big crisis. So there is no better time to be trying to do what I can to support the next generation of young people," she says.She added that while Burnham may not be welcome on her YouTube series, she would "100% love to have a conversation with him" about what he's doing to tackle youth unemployment."I think having more training schemes, apprenticeships is really, really vital in helping young people," she says.Away from her Academy, Dimoldenberg is hugely busy building her media empire.The second series of Passenger Princess, her comedy series which sees her interview some of Formula 1's biggest names while learning how to drive, has just dropped on YouTube.She also hosts red carpet interviews at the Oscars - following a tried-and-tested formula of comedic flirting and uncomfortable silences - and runs her own production company.But she doesn't take any of it for granted. Before going on a red carpet, she does copious amounts of research. "[It's] like you're really studying for your A-levels again," she said. "I make sure that I have specific questions for every single person that I might meet."Next up, she's starring in a rom-com - "playing myself", she says, angelically - and says she wants to do more directing, having recently got behind the camera for Maisie Peters' music video for single My Regards.Meanwhile, Chicken Shop Date continues to go from strength to strength.The show is billed around interviewing musicians, actors and comedians over a plate of nuggets. Politicians don't really make the cut (it's not just Burnham), and neither does royalty ("the Royals are just not really my type either".)Her chemistry with the Spider-Man actor Andrew Garfield sent the internet into meltdown, and led to speculation that they were romantically linked in real life. When asked why that didn't work out, Dimoldenberg says she was too busy and "just couldn't make the time," but she is sanguine about it. "You know, these things happen," she muses.So what's next for Dimoldenberg? I wonder whether she has her eyes on a pivot to a traditional TV couch format - perhaps picking up from Claudia Winkleman, whose show ended after one series - but she doesn't seem interested."I feel like what I have with Chicken Shop Date is essentially a late night talk show," she says."And I think that there wouldn't really be a need for me to do something other than that right now while I have Chicken Shop Date, because to me it serves the purpose of what a chat show is."Dimoldenberg has previously indicated that she will close the shop when she gets the Canadian rapper Drake on her show."Well, the stars haven't aligned yet, but you never know what might happen in the future," she says of her Drake bid. "Maybe I have to go to Toronto, but no, I'd much rather he come to me."For now though, she bats away any suggestion that she's ready to end her series, even though she's arguably now more famous than some of the people she interviews."I still feel like there are dates that I really want to do," she says."I need fall in love, you know? I need to meet my one true love. So I have to carry on until that happens."

schema.headline: Chicken Shop Date's Amelia Dimoldenberg: I wouldn't invite Andy Burnham on my show - but I'd love a chat

title: Limiting sugar before age two linked to better brain health
description: "They may be onto something," said Rachel Richardson, the methods support unit lead for evidence production and methods directorate at Cochrane, an in
body: "They may be onto something," said Rachel Richardson, the methods support unit lead for evidence production and methods directorate at Cochrane, an independent non-profit network that gathers and summarises medical research.However, she said this "does not represent a smoking gun" linking early sugar intake to dementia.One big issue is, it is impossible to know how much sugar each of the people in the study were actually eating, merely when they were born relative to sugar rationing. "This evidence relates to people born in the 1940s and 1950s and so its applicability to young children today is limited - for example, weaning took place earlier and this would have a large impact on the early nutrition of babies and children," said Richardson. Prof Ian Maidment, professor of clinical pharmacy at Aston University, said: "It is an interesting idea, it helps inform debate, but in my opinion we need more evidence."He said connecting "something that happened 80 years ago" and projecting that onto health now meant there were "loads" of other factors that could be playing a role. Dr Sara Rodrigues, from Alzheimer's Research UK, said: "It's important to remember that this was an observational study."This means it can identify links between diet and dementia risk, but it cannot prove that eating less sugar directly prevents dementia."Eating a healthy, balanced diet is one of the best ways to support your brain health and it's never too late to make positive changes."

schema.headline: Limiting sugar before age two linked to better brain health

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Kate O'Connor wins NI's first gold in heptathlon
description: O'Connor was favourite heading into the event after the late withdrawal of England's Katarina Johnson-Thompson, who beat her to gold in 2022, and she
body: O'Connor was favourite heading into the event after the late withdrawal of England's Katarina Johnson-Thompson, who beat her to gold in 2022, and she certainly lived up to the billing.The Newry-born athlete led after the first two events on Tuesday. She ran the 100m hurdles in 13.54 seconds and produced a season's best 1.82m in the high jump.In a rain-soaked evening session she dipped in the shot put, throwing just 12.85 in difficult conditions.While she said she was "gutted" with that performance, she rallied and she bounced back well to run the 200m in a season's best time of 24.14, which was just 0.07 off her personal best as she strolled to victory in her heat.She earned 3,731 points across the four events to top the standings heading into Wednesday's second day of the competition and, with a 49-point advantage over O'Dowda, looked to be in pole position for gold.O'Connor further increased that lead on Wednesday morning as she recorded a leap of 1.82m in the long jump and a season's best 52.85m in the javelin to move 258 points ahead.In the 800m, she finished first as she ran 2:10.45 to take home NI's first multi-class gold medal since Dame Mary Peters won the pentathlon in 1974.Her NI team-mate Anna McCauley finished eighth in the standings, despite being second-fastest in the 800m behind O'Connor.O'Connor will receive her gold medal on Thursday at 18:30 BST.

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Kate O'Connor wins NI's first gold in heptathlon

title: Saltburn Cricket Club: Jonathan Agnew on 'finger-clicking' scandal
description: Everyone seems to have formed their own opinion on the alleged cheating scandal enveloping Saltburn Cricket Club, and it's not hard to see why.I've ha
body: Everyone seems to have formed their own opinion on the alleged cheating scandal enveloping Saltburn Cricket Club, and it's not hard to see why.I've had countless messages today from people who are intrigued by the whole thing. Many are from people who don't usually message me about cricket.It's a perfect social media story which does the rounds very quickly and people quickly reach their own opinion.At the centre of it all is the suggestion a second XI player from Saltburn Cricket Club, Brian Devine, clicked his fingers the moment the ball passed the bat of an opponent, thus making it sound like the ball had hit the edge.Cricket scandal stories always grab people's attention and this one is the sort of incident in which people who are not interested in cricket can get involved – did he click his fingers or did he not? Could the umpire hear it or could he not?It's one of those simple things that anybody can engage with. It's not as complicated as assessing whether a footballer has dived – this is a cut and dried thing that anybody can enter a debate into.People seem to enjoy a Spirit of Cricket debate - it's part of the fabric of the game and almost unique to the sport.Devine, who has been suspended by his club,, external must have a proper hearing and tell his side of the story. People have come to conclusions very quickly and maybe they're right but until there's been a proper investigation, it's difficult to pass judgement.For me, the wicketkeeper, Josh Bowes, is the person who will ultimately know what happened. Unless Devine confesses to anything, the wicketkeeper is the star witness for the prosecution and the defence. It's up to him to be honest.Bearing in mind all of us are reaching judgements from some pretty grainy video, if Devine is seriously managing to click his fingers so loudly the umpire can hear it outside, with everything else that is going on, then he clearly has to be punished.Anybody who is caught cheating in any sport takes that risk. They take the risk of being exposed as a cheat and they'll be punished as a cheat.Then there's the decision to be made about the team itself and whether other people knew about it and were part of it.But that can only happen after there has been a proper hearing and proper process.Let's be frank though, these things do happen in cricket - people are always pushing to try and gain an advantage. The only sport I am aware of where it doesn't happen, and I'd happily stand corrected here, is golf, because of its self-policing nature.Whenever you have an umpire or referee to try and con as a player, then this sort of thing goes on.In my playing days, I remember standing at first slip in a county match when West Indies fast bowler Andy Roberts was playing for us [Leicestershire].The wicketkeeper at the time, who I won't name, ran on the spot very loudly in a distracting fashion as the bowler was running in. After he did it a couple of times, the batsman turned round and told him in no uncertain terms if he did it again, he would do something rather uncomfortable with his cricket bat.We've had ball-tampering scandals – all of these things – and they all fall under the same bracket of foul play and bringing the game into disrepute.What I would say is the whole Spirit of Cricket question is an incredibly difficult path to tread. These things happen and everybody has different views.It starts with everybody having a different perspective or interpretation of the Spirit of Cricket and very few people agree on that. Then it kicks off from there. It's extraordinarily difficult to get a consensus on these things.But it goes on everywhere, all around the world. I know it's been a big story in Australia too but I've played grade cricket in Australia and I think I'm pretty experienced in knowing how Australians play their grade cricket.Their league cricket is utterly uncompromising, it's ruthless and I've certainly seen evidence of sharp practice in the two or three seasons I played there.It's not the first incident and it won't be the last. What's important now is that we get a full and fair investigation.Jonathan Agnew was talking to BBC Sport's Marc Higginson

schema.headline: Saltburn Cricket Club: Jonathan Agnew on 'finger-clicking' scandal

title: Two firefighters die in Crete as wildfires threaten parts of southern Europe
description: Two Greek firefighters have died after they became trapped tackling a wildfire that swept through the Rethymno area of Crete.Gale-force winds whipped
body: Two Greek firefighters have died after they became trapped tackling a wildfire that swept through the Rethymno area of Crete.Gale-force winds whipped up the flames prompting the evacuation of several villages, in the latest summer wildfire to break out in southern Europe.In southern Turkey, the main Fethiye to Antalya highway had to be closed and part of a hospital evacuated because of a fire in Muğla province.Meanwhile, a fourth heatwave of the summer has begun in Spain and France, and firefighters are trying to prevent a flare-up from major wildfires that have just been brought under control.Witnesses said several fires broke out on Crete and spread fast, with the worst fire front extending as far as 15km (9.3 miles). The fire department said the two men who died were working near the western city of Rethymno.Wildfires have also broken out elsewhere in Greece, on the islands of Paros and Lesbos in the Aegean Sea, and the southern town of Trifylia on the Greek mainland.In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has warned the next 12 hours will be "decisive" in putting out a wildfire near the capital Madrid. "Things are progressing favourably, with maximum caution," he told reporters, because of higher temperatures, lower humidity and the risk of gusts of wind.More than 43,000 hectares (108,000 acres) has already burned at Burgohondo in Ávila province, 150km (93 miles) west of Madrid. It is now considered the largest recorded wildfire in Spanish history.  In total this year more than 207,000 hectares of land have been burned by wildfires in Spain.One of the team directing firefighting operations, Francisco Bolaños, said that while the fire had not "moved a centimetre during the night", there were concerns it could re-ignite because of the higher temperatures, and the focus was on stabilising a perimeter of 180km (112 miles). Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world, and Europe is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's water supply, and more intense wildfires.In south-west France, the largest fires in the Gironde region are described as "still stabilised" despite several flare-ups, however officials warn of dry winds and temperatures of up to 41C (106F).The mayor of Le Barp, south-west of Bordeaux, Blandine Sarrazin, warned that the situation was "getting harder", after two fires had broken out the day before, and said everyone had to be "hyper-vigilant".

schema.headline: Two firefighters die in Crete as wildfires threaten parts of southern Europe

title: Stephen Fleming: England expected to appoint former New Zealand captain as Test coach
description: Fleming would inherit a side that saw its momentum falter after a breathtaking start to the McCullum era. McCullum won 10 out of 12 Tests in his first
body: Fleming would inherit a side that saw its momentum falter after a breathtaking start to the McCullum era. McCullum won 10 out of 12 Tests in his first year in charge but since then, England have lost 18 and won 17 of 37 Tests.They have not won a multi-match series since December 2024. It is unclear whether Fleming would be in position to lead England in the three-Test series against Pakistan, which gets under way at Headingley on 19 August, or wait until December's tour of South Africa. Assistant coach Marcus Trescothick and former skipper Joe Root, who led the side in Stokes' absence in the second Test against New Zealand, could fill the roles of head coach and captain, respectively, on an interim basis., externalHarry Brook is the current England vice-captain and received "100%" backing from Stokes to become his successor. However the 27-year-old, who leads the white-ball sides, was overlooked for the role earlier in the summer.His involvement in a nightclub incident last winter, when he was punched by a bouncer on the eve of a one-day international, was a contributing factor in that decision. In addition to Flower, former Australian head coach Justin Langer was also expected to be a top contender for the England role. However, on a recent appearance on the Stick to Cricket podcast, Langer said he had not been contacted by the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB).Former England batter Jonathan Trott, Richard Dawson, Gareth Batty and Australians Tom Moody, Darren Lehmann and Ryan Campbell were among the other names linked to the role.The decision to remove McCullum came after the ECB hierarchy spent time reflecting on the situation surrounding the men's team, with the 4-1 Ashes hammering in Australia followed by a 2-1 home series defeat by New Zealand, including Stokes announcing his retirement during play in the third Test.Former England and Kent batter Key was backed to retain his position following the Ashes and defeat by New Zealand. Key and a headhunting company conducted interviews with potential candidates. Unlike many of McCullum's other potential successors, Fleming has never previously worked as head coach of a national team.However, since retiring from playing in 2009, he has been in demand on the franchise circuit, most notably enjoying a 17-year tenure as head coach of Indian Premier League (IPL) franchise Chennai Super Kings.Fleming led CSK to five IPL titles from nine finals and two Champions League T20 crowns, as well as taking the helm at sister sides Texas Super Kings in Major League Cricket and Joburg Super Kings in SA20.The 53-year-old also spent two seasons in charge of Southern Brave in The Hundred, reaching the final in 2024.No stranger to Test cricket, he made 111 appearances for New Zealand, scoring over 7,000 runs at 40.06, and remains the Black Caps' most successful captain with 28 wins from 80 matches.Nor is he a stranger to the county game having spent time with Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire - where he won the County Championship in 2005.

schema.headline: Stephen Fleming: England expected to appoint former New Zealand captain as Test coach

title: France fire crews battle heat as locals tell BBC of fight to save homes
description: As the smoke eases, firefighters then move into the forest on foot to try and contain the latest flare-up.They are the principal concern for the thous
body: As the smoke eases, firefighters then move into the forest on foot to try and contain the latest flare-up.They are the principal concern for the thousands of crews and volunteers combating the wildfires that have raged here for a week, forcing tens of thousands of residents and tourists to flee.As temperatures peak at around 40C, fires restarting on their own are a constant threat.After 20 minutes or so, the one we are watching is brought under control, only for another to suddenly emerge on the opposite side of the road."Leave now!" shouts an understandably irritable officer as he drives past. The smoke is becoming thicker and more aggressive. Indeed, time to leave.Such is the vast scale of the infernos ravaging France's south-western Gironde region, that it is not always obvious what direction the smoke is coming from.It simply descends as you travel west from Bordeaux along empty roads and through deserted villages.The soil is powder-like and covered in endless pinecones and dried leaves. It explains how the wildfires have spread at the rate they have."If it's too late, at least we tried," said a defiant Hugo, 26, as he refilled his water tank. "Fifty thousand hectares has already been destroyed, what will we tell our children?"Hugo grew up in the area and has returned from his home in Bali to watch his mother's house in the village of Arès, which is perilously close to the wildfires."It's horrible, it's our home, it's our region, it's our forest, it's where we grew up, it's where our family live, where we live, it's horrible. I feel a lot of sadness," Maëlys, 23, told us, her face covered in soot."I am a nurse and I'm here to help," she added. Maëlys said her friends own big water tanks, which they then use to try to put out fires that flare-up to prevent them from spreading."In the morning I am at the hospital working, and in the afternoon I'm in the forest helping," she said.

schema.headline: France fire crews battle heat as locals tell BBC of fight to save homes

title: Social care reform: The families hoping for change
description: 'Every day I'm just winging it': The families hoping for social care reformImage source, Emma RileyImage caption, Emma Riley is a dental nurse from Ma
body: 'Every day I'm just winging it': The families hoping for social care reformImage source, Emma RileyImage caption, Emma Riley is a dental nurse from Manchester, as was her mother Carol before she retired ByRozina SiniBBC Your VoiceJim ReedHealth reporter and Paul GribbenAndy Burnham has pledged to reform the adult social care system in England, meeting the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to try to find "common ground" on the issue.He wants an independent review of care to be brought forward by a year to 2027, as well as major reforms to pay and conditions for staff and the creation of a national care service.But the prime minister said "difficult decisions" would have to be made on tax to fund sustainable change, adding that in an "ideal world" no-one should have to sell their home to pay for care.BBC Your Voice has been speaking to families affected by what they see as shortfalls in the system.'Quietly confident'Emma Riley has been caring for her mother Carol, who has dementia, since she lost her father 18 months ago."She's a cracking lady, still with a sense of humour but she's living with this awful condition," said Riley, from Manchester.She is paying £34 an hour for a care company to come to the house three times a week, which she describes as a "huge chunk of money" although she is happy with the level of care.Riley wants to keep her mum in the family home, but the caring commitments affect her job as a dental nurse.She started applying to the local council for funding to support her mother at home at the beginning of the year, but six months on, she is still waiting for a final decision. "It's not the social worker's fault, it is just the caseload," she said. Riley called for more communication to help her navigate the system, adding: "I'm blindly going through it at the moment."Every day I'm just winging it but there's a human being upstairs."Riley said she heard the prime minister's speech and it had left her feeling "quietly confident". Burnham has announced that a review of social care by veteran Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey would now be published next summer."I do think Baroness Casey will make the changes we need," Riley added.'Tough decisions'Image source, Family handoutImage caption, The Greenwood family in West Yorkshire say they have had to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for their mother, MavisLisa Greenwood, from Halifax, West Yorkshire, said she would be supportive of the prime minister if he managed to change how the care sector operates. "It does need changing and hopefully it will get better," she said. Greenwood said her family is having to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for her mother, Mavis, who is 90 and in local respite care. It is costing £1,305 a week, something Greenwood says the family "cannot sustain". She said they now face the prospect of having to sell her mother's home, describing this as "very distressing".Greenwood backs Burnham's proposal to increase pay in the sector and suggests it will help attract more staff."Carers do need to be paid more," she said. "There are some fantastic people doing the job on little wages." Greenwood told the BBC's Your Voice that both her parents had worked "all their lives saving for the future". "Yet here we are in a situation of stress not knowing how we are going to continue with mum in the home," she added. "We can't give up our jobs, we need to work to pay our bills."'Left to figure things out'Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Sophie and her father Stephen, who died in 2024 when she was just 16Sophie Daniels was 16 when her father died in 2024 as a result of stage 4 glioblastoma, a highly aggressive brain tumour. The 18-year-old felt that there was a lack of support for her family. Along with her mother and sister, she looked after her father at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, as "social care provision was incredibly limited".Daniels said: "We hardly had any help and we were left to figure things out ourselves. "Thankfully, charities helped us with that but towards the end my mum had to give up work to care for my dad."She said that one of the biggest practical challenges her family faced was a lack of a lifting service to help him move around the house.  "He fell fairly frequently and a lack of lifting service meant that our dad was forced to either wait for hours on the floor for an ambulance or for us to try and use techniques to pull my dad up."'Not easy to solve'Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andy Burnham made his speech at a north London care home, where he spoke to some of the residentsSteve West, from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, cared for his mother for many years before taking the difficult decision to place her in a care home. She died earlier this year.West, 64, said he was "frustrated hearing the same issues that need fixing being discussed by each new government".Listening to the prime minister's speech, he said that a proposed national care service "could give focus, but its remit needs to be confirmed". "I think a cross-party approach would be a benefit as the plans would take a few terms of parliament at least and then to maintain the benefits for years to come," he added.He said when caring for his mother, the biggest challenge was "knowing who to speak to" and "dealing with several health bodies", sometimes having to repeat her medical history several times.  "She got progressively worse and I remember one time sitting in a car park for an hour-and-a-half trying to get an emergency social worker," he said, adding that "having a system that is unified would be a massive help". West believes the prime minister "needs to focus on one or two big-ticket items - those that will have the biggest impact". He said if relatives caring for loved ones were paid at similar rates to private companies, "perhaps more people would feel they were able to provide support" as they would not be negatively impacted by cutting work hours or leaving their jobs. 'A terrible time for the family'Image source, Jeanette BarryImage caption, John Barry was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died from the disease in 2024. Pictured here with his wife Jeanette.Jeanette Barry from Essex was married to her husband John for 42 years before he was diagnosed with dementia in 2018. The former policeman was moved to a local care home as his needs became more complex. "At one point he was roaming the streets at night because he thought he was still on duty," said Barry."I couldn't keep him in the house, so at 2am or 3am I was having to follow him to make sure he was alright."She paid £2,000 a month in care home fees out of her husband's police pension, on top of local authority funding, although she didn't "begrudge a penny of that money" as he was well looked after.She says she was told by one social worker that she would have to remortgage her house or her husband would be moved to another care home, but he was later reassessed and qualified for more financial support."I had to think twice before putting my heating on," she says. "It was a horrible, terrible time for the family."Barry, whose husband died two years ago, said she doesn't have much faith in politicians to make the social care system work, but noted the prime minister has experience of the matter as his father has Alzheimer's. "They all make promises but then they never do anything," she said. "I have slightly more confidence in Andy Burnham because he has personal experience of dementia but how is he going to pay for it?"

schema.headline: Social care reform: The families hoping for change

title: In pictures: Scale of drought across England as rivers dry up
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A golfing green surrounded by dried grass in Dorset, just one of the areas declared to be in drought on Wedne
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A golfing green surrounded by dried grass in Dorset, just one of the areas declared to be in drought on WednesdayByMatthew TuckerDrought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.The announcement means there have been three droughts in the past five years - 2022, 2025 and now 2026.Photos from across the country have captured some of the dry conditions - including receding rivers, parched parks and sportspeople trying to play on.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesThere is no single definition of drought, but it usually refers to a period of prolonged unusually dry weather that can have impacts on people, nature and the environment.A lack of rainfall has meant rivers have lowered, including the River Thames, exposing the riverbed in London.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesThe river height marker was left completely dry at a ford on the River Redlake in Bucknell, Shropshire.Image source, Getty ImagesThe riverbed of the River Wye in Hereford was seen bare after weeks without rainfall.Image source, Getty ImagesSome areas of the country have now entered their fourth heatwave of the year.Beauty spots and parks have been left yellow and parched, including London's Greenwich Park, Blackheath, Primrose Hill, Hackney Marshes, Peckham Common and Leyton Flats.Image source, EPAImage source, EPAImage source, ShutterstockImage source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesWhile droughts happen naturally, scientists say that climate change is raising the risks, with higher summer temperatures drying out soils more quickly. This can lead to more severe and longer-lasting droughts.Image source, EPAThe sight of scorched brown leaves has become a familiar view.Image source, Getty ImagesHollow Pond in East London was seen diminished in size.Image source, EPAImage source, EPAAnd golfers at Woldingham Golf Club found their normally lush course had turned to patches of green.Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesSimilarly, a shrinking island of green was played on by cricketers as Maidenhead & Bray club took on Boyne Hill in the village of Bray in Berkshire.Image source, Getty ImagesReservoirs have also shrunk, including the Walthamstow Wetlands.Image source, Getty ImagesAnd Howden Reservoir in the Upper Derwent Valley in the Peak District has receding shores.Image source, EPA

title: James Desborough given whole life orders for Cornwall double murders
description: Serial killer given whole life orders for murdering two menImage source, Devon and Cornwall PoliceImage caption, James Desborough was on Tuesday found
body: Serial killer given whole life orders for murdering two menImage source, Devon and Cornwall PoliceImage caption, James Desborough was on Tuesday found guilty of murdering two men he met at a homeless shelterByJohanna Carrat Winchester Crown Court and Julia GregorySouth WestUpdated 4 hours agoSerial killer James Desborough has been given two whole life prison sentences with no chance of parole - as police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that housed him.Desborough, already serving a minimum of 19 years for the murder of his prison cellmate, was given the whole life tariffs for killing 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall.Aquilino and Coleman met Desborough at Newquay's Sandy Lodge homeless shelter, where police are now reviewing the unexplained deaths of two other men and two women.Sentencing, Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini described Desborough, 40, as "a highly dangerous individual who had no regard for the life of those you think are worthless".Desborough befriended the two vulnerable men and used "extreme violence" on both of them, before dismembering and concealing their bodies, the judge said. He said the former builder used their bank cards and made journeys to give the impression they were still alive.Image source, Devon and Cornwall PoliceImage caption, The remains of Daniel Coleman and Claudio Aquilino were found in Cornish woodland Their remains were discovered close to Desborough's woodland cabin near Sticker in Cornwall.It was while he was on remand charged with their murders that he strangled his cellmate, Steven Kempster, at HMP Exeter.The judge at Winchester Crown Court said the offences had an exceptionally high level of seriousness and it was rare to impose such a sentence with no chance of parole.Desborough was also sentenced to five years on each count of preventing the lawful burial of Aquilino and Coleman, who were last seen alive on 18 April 2025 and on 3 June 2025 respectively.Figure caption, Police arrest triple murderer James Desborough in his woodland cabinIn victim impact statements read out in court, Coleman and Aquilino's families spoke of their anguish imagining the pain and fear the men suffered.Coleman's brother, Tony Nye, said there "weren't enough words in the English language" to describe the suffering Desborough had caused his family."You have taken from this world my big brother in the most disgusting and horrific way," he said."The world will see you for the vile degenerate coward you are. There will be no forgiveness for you in this world or the next."His mother, Sandra Coleman, said: "You took my firstborn son. You destroyed any hope of us coming together as a family. "You have given me a life sentence of pain, despair, anxiety and hopelessness."Image source, Devon and Cornwall Police/PA WireImage caption, Police found items belonging to both men hidden in Desborough's woodland cabin Aquilino's uncle David Bonomi said his nephew was a "friendly, talented artist" who had been killed in a "brutal, cruel and evil manner".He said the family had reported him missing as it was "very unusual for him not to have been in contact" as he called his mother every day.Speaking earlier about the review of the four unexplained deaths, Det Supt Rachael Bentley, from Devon and Cornwall Police, said: "As a major crime investigation team we were informed by the coroner's officer for His Majesty's Coroner that there were four deaths at Sandy Lodge."As part of the investigation, a detective inspector, separate to the investigation but within major crime, did a review of those deaths, and that included commissioning some more forensic work, some CCTV, and statements."Inquiries were ongoing and Desborough was "not a suspect at this time", Bentley said."We don't believe there is a link at this time, but I said it's an ongoing investigation," she added.Image source, Devon and Cornwall PoliceImage caption, Police found bone fragments and body parts in woodland near Desborough's cabinBentley said police attended each of the deaths at Sandy Lodge and inquiries suggested natural causes but coronial investigations were paused when Desborough was arrested for murder.Desborough dismembered Coleman and Aquilino's bodies, tried to burn their remains and hid them in woodland in Sticker.As part of a lengthy search of dense laurel and bogland involving about 100 officers, police found thousands of bone fragments in a stream and body parts in a shallow grave.Several handwritten notes were also found inside the cabin, including one headed "Bug out list", another "Hostiles" and a diagram labelled "Kill Zone".Image source, Devon and Cornwall PoliceImage caption, Handwritten notes were found inside the cabinClosing the case to the jury, Ahmed Hossain KC, said Desborough was capable of switching to "very serious violence".Bentley described the killings as "callous and cold-blooded", as "both men were vulnerable and trusted James Desborough as their friend" before he brutally murdered them and "savagely desecrated their bodies".Desborough killed Kempster in Exeter Prison on 15 September 2025, just three days after they started sharing a cell.The court heard Desborough was irritated by his cellmate's snoring and returning of unwashed cutlery.The night before the murder he warned he would kill him if he continued to snore.Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

title: More than half of England in drought, Environment Agency declares
description: The combination of low rainfall and prolonged high temperatures - meaning greater evaporation of moisture - has quickly depleted water reserves in soi
body: The combination of low rainfall and prolonged high temperatures - meaning greater evaporation of moisture - has quickly depleted water reserves in soils, vegetation and rivers. These conditions have led to a "flash drought", the EA has said. This is where drought begins suddenly rather than over many months or years.Today's announcement means there have been three droughts in the past five years – 2022, 2025 and now 2026.While droughts happen naturally, scientists say that climate change is raising the risks, with higher summer temperatures drying out soils more quickly. This can lead to more severe and longer-lasting droughts.Some researchers have also highlighted underinvestment in water infrastructure as an issue.The EA has previously warned that England's public water supplies could face a shortfall of 5 billion litres per day by the middle of the century without urgent action."This drought isn't just about a lack of rain," said Prof Hayley Fowler of Newcastle University. "It's the result of hotter temperatures from a warming climate, rising water demand, ageing infrastructure and too much water being lost through leaks."The government has committed to improving the water industry and water companies have announced plans for investment, but bills are rising as a result.The dry conditions have consequences for nature, with Atlantic salmon unable to move upstream where river flows are low. Agriculture has also taken a hit. Paul Tompkins, deputy president of the National Farmers' Union of England and Wales (NFU), said: "Farmers and growers have always had to contend with the weather, but what they are experiencing now is climate change in action. More extreme conditions [are] making it harder, riskier and more costly to produce the nation's food."He added the issue of drought is something that "should matter to everyone" as it affects the country's food security. Some areas of the country have now entered their fourth heatwave of the year. Amber and yellow heat health alerts have come into force for parts of the UK, with temperatures potentially peaking at 35C in parts of south-east England on Wednesday. The hot, dry weather has created ideal conditions for wildfires to spread. The National Fire Chiefs Council has warned that wildfire risk "remains elevated across the UK". More than 200 wildfire incidents have been reported in England and Wales over the past two weeks, it said.The Met Office has separately announced that the new June temperature record set last month was even higher than previously thought, following verification processes.The previously-reported figure of 37.7C in Lingwood, Norfolk, on 26 June 2026 has been updated to 38.0C – smashing the UK's previous June high of 35.6C.Additional reporting by Jess Carr

title: World Cup 2026: Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina
description: Fifa has opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over their behaviour after their World Cup final loss to Spain and throughout the tournamen
body: Fifa has opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over their behaviour after their World Cup final loss to Spain and throughout the tournament.Last week, the world governing body appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at the New York New Jersey Stadium, with multiple Argentina players and backroom staff involved in altercations with Spain players following their 1-0 loss in July.On the recommendation of the prosecutor, Fifa will investigate Argentina players Nahuel Molina (two counts) and Leandro Paredes (three counts), and Argentina assistant coach Roberto Ayala (one count) for alleged assault under article 14 of Fifa's disciplinary code.Molina may also face disciplinary action for one count of alleged unsporting behaviour under article 14. Team-mate Thiago Almada and Spain midfielder Gavi are also accused of the same breach.Under Fifa's disciplinary code, players and officials face at least a one-match suspension for unsportsmanlike conduct and at least three matches for assault.
